```json
{"claims":[{"claim_text":"From roughly 1945 to the 1970s, the United States and non-Communist Europe experienced solid economic growth.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"From roughly 1945 to the 1970s, the United States and non-Communist Europe experienced declining inequality.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"From roughly 1945 to the 1970s, the United States and non-Communist Europe experienced expanding social services.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"From roughly 1945 to the 1970s, the United States and non-Communist Europe experienced increasing working-class power.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"From roughly 1945 to the 1970s, the United States and non-Communist Europe experienced landmark advances toward racial, gender and sexual equality.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"In countries such as France and Sweden, labor and socialist movements made significant progress toward a democratic socialist transition.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"Starting in the 1970s, economic elites in the United States and non-Communist Europe began mobilizing politically to lower taxes for the rich and corporations.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"Starting in the 1970s, economic elites in the United States and non-Communist Europe began mobilizing politically to eviscerate democratic decision-making both in the workplace and at the ballot box.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"Starting in the 1970s, economic elites in the United States and non-Communist Europe began mobilizing politically to slash spending on essential social services such as education and social security.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"Starting in the 1970s, economic elites in the United States and non-Communist Europe began mobilizing politically to deregulate industries across the economy.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"Starting in the 1970s, economic elites in the United States and non-Communist Europe began mobilizing politically to open up flows of capital across national borders.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"These actions enabled corporations to evade accountability to the workers they employed and to the communities in which they operated.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"In the United States, neoliberalism was aided by racialized attacks on social service provision.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"In the United States, African American and Latino recipients of welfare and other anti-poverty programs were portrayed as an “undeserving poor” whose lifestyle was being subsidized by white taxpayers.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"The success of neoliberalism across the United States and Europe differed based upon the relative strength or weakness of left-wing political parties and trade unions.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"Working people in traditional bastions of social democracy such as Sweden were relatively better off than working people in countries such as the United States where trade unions and the Left have been weak historically.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]},{"claim_text":"By the early 2000s, the historic gains made across these countries in the post-World War Two period had been rolled back dramatically.",
"claim_types":["factual_assertion"],"evidence_ids":[1]}],"unresolved_references":[]}
```
